issues.description: The manuscript presents inferential results and substantive conclusions in the abstract and results, but repeatedly states that the data are randomized/dummy data generated to simulate output before actual data collection. This makes the reported findings non-empirical and invalidates any interpretation as a replication or extension result.
issues.quote: [IMPORTANT: Results were written using randomized dataset produced by Qualtrics to simulate what these sections will look like after data collection. These will be updated following the data collection.] ... We generated a dummy set of samples in the Qualtrics survey (N = 1000) and found no empirical support for the effect of analytical reasoning on the identifiable victim effect.

issues.description: The methods and results are explicitly based on randomized simulated Qualtrics data rather than real participant data, yet the manuscript proceeds as if reporting a completed empirical study. This is a fundamental internal inconsistency that prevents evaluation of the actual replication.
issues.quote: [IMPORTANT: Method and results sections were written using randomized dataset produced by Qualtrics to simulate what these sections will look like after data collection. These will be updated following the data collection.]

issues.description: The sample consists of generated responses rather than human participants. Therefore, exclusion criteria, demographics, power, attention checks, and all statistical tests are meaningless for evaluating the target effect.
issues.quote: A total of 1000 responses were generated from the Qualtrics for pre-registration (Mage = 67.80, SD=30.10; 471 females and 529 males).

issues.subcategory: changed design from between-subjects to within-subjects
issues.description: The manuscript states that Studies 1 and 3 were embedded into a single within-subject design, which is a major departure from the original random-assignment design. Exposure to multiple victim conditions within the same participant can itself induce comparison, deliberation, demand, carryover, and contrast effects, particularly fatal for a phenomenon theorized to depend on separate versus joint evaluation.
issues.quote: We embedded Studies 1 and 3 of Small et al. (2007) into a single within-subject design with identifiability and intervention as the independent variables; donation and feeling variables as the dependent variables respectively.

issues.description: The manuscript first describes the original studies as randomly assigning participants, but in the replication procedure states that participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions. Self-selection destroys experimental control and is incompatible with ANOVA assumptions for randomized groups. It also contradicts the claimed replication design.
issues.quote: Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions.

issues.description: If participants selected their own conditions, any differences between conditions are confounded with participant preferences, prior attitudes, or motivations. Causal claims about intervention or identifiability effects would therefore be invalid.
issues.quote: Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions.

issues.subcategory: within-subject design inconsistent with cell counts
issues.description: The reported sample sizes per cell sum to 1000 across six cells, implying each participant appears in exactly one cell, which is consistent with a between-subjects design, not the stated within-subject design. The design description and descriptive tables cannot both be correct.
issues.quote: We embedded Studies 1 and 3 of Small et al. (2007) into a single within-subject design...

issues.description: The cell counts across the 2×3 design sum to 1000 (159+175+166+175+159+166), indicating participants were partitioned into separate groups rather than measured repeatedly across conditions. This conflicts with the declared within-subject design.

The replication changes multiple core features simultaneously: combines two studies, adds intervention to the joint condition, changes donation from real to hypothetical, moves from lab to MTurk/online, updates victim materials, removes earning and donating actual money, and measures additional outcomes. These deviations alter the psychological meaning of the task and undermine the claim of a close/very close replication.
issues.quote: In this replication, we merged Studies 1 and 3 into one single experiment... The intervention of learning about the effect would also be applied to the joint condition... Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 to the corresponding victim(s) instead of donating the money to Save the Children after signing a charity request letter.

issues.description: The original paradigm involved consequential charitable giving with actual money. Replacing this with an imaginary donation changes the dependent variable from behavior to stated intention/hypothetical preference, which may engage different motives and weakens construct validity for charitable giving and the identifiable victim effect.
issues.quote: Imaginary donation Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 to the corresponding victim(s) instead of donating the money to Save the Children after signing a charity request letter.

issues.description: The manuscript frames the mechanism as deliberative/calculative/analytical thinking, but the explicit manipulation is described as learning about the identifiable victim effect from prior research. Being told about a bias is not the same construct as inducing deliberative thought, and the implicit joint-presentation manipulation is also conceptually distinct. This blurs what is being tested.
issues.quote: participants under manipulation were taught about the identifiable victim effect before donating to the victims... We modify the original hypotheses for the interaction effect of explicit or implicit intervention on the donation tendency of different victim groups

issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly describes the joint condition as participants 'implicitly learning about the identifiable victim effect.' Joint evaluation may alter evaluation mode, but it does not teach or constitute learning about the effect. This confuses theoretical mechanism and manipulation.
issues.quote: 4 (Interaction effect) | Implicitly learning about the identifiable victim effect reduces donations to an identifiable victim

issues.description: The introduction makes broad normative claims about unfairness and efficient social resource allocation as if these are established implications of the effect. These claims are philosophical/policy assertions not directly tested here and may bias framing of the phenomenon.
issues.quote: The inconsistent prosocial motivation not only demonstrates human sense of unfairness in valuing life, but also highlights the lack of efficiency in resource allocation when asserts are accumulated on a single victim instead of dispersing to a greater population to benefit the society as a whole.

issues.subcategory: power analysis omitted from main text
issues.description: The manuscript claims the sample size was determined by power analysis, but does not report the target effect size, alpha, desired power, test family, tails, design assumptions, or resulting required N in the manuscript itself. This prevents evaluation of whether the study was truly well-powered, especially given the altered design.
issues.quote: To obtain the minimal sample size required for this study, The sample size for this study was determined to ensure adequate statistical power for detecting the effects reported in the original study. The full report of power analysis can be found in the supplementary

issues.subcategory: design and analysis changed from original without clear justification
issues.description: The manuscript departs from the original analyses by not conducting the ordered probit regression used in the original and by adding multiple ANOVAs/post hocs across many outcomes. These changes increase researcher degrees of freedom, especially with an ordinal 0-5 donation outcome, but are not justified in terms of statistical appropriateness or preregistered priority.
issues.quote: Ordered probit regression ... This test would not be conducted in the replication

issues.subcategory: ordinal outcome analyzed as continuous without justification
issues.description: Donation appears to be an integer from $0 to $5, which is a bounded ordinal/count-like outcome. The original study reportedly used ordered probit regression, but the replication drops it and uses ANOVA/t-tests without justification or robustness checks. This may distort inference and comparability to the original.
issues.quote: Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 ... Ordered probit regression ... This test would not be conducted in the replication

issues.subcategory: means reported in text do not match table
issues.description: The narrative interpretation of the significant identifiability effect gives means that do not correspond to the descriptive table. Table 7 reports identifiable M=2.54 and statistical M=2.23 when collapsed across intervention, but the text reverses them and reports different values. This casts doubt on the correctness of analyses and interpretation.
issues.quote: participants who faced a statistical victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67).

issues.description: The post-hoc contrast is reported as Identifiable vs Statistical, t(994) = -2.40, implying the first mean is lower than the second, but the text's means are inconsistent and Table 7 suggests a smaller difference in the opposite labels used in the text. This indicates likely coding or reporting errors in condition labels.

A negative t-statistic for Identifiable vs Statistical is paired with a positive Cohen's d and a confidence interval spanning negative to positive values but interpreted as significant. The sign convention is unclear and the reported CI for d is inconsistent with p=.049 because it includes zero. Either the effect size, CI, or p-value is wrong.

issues.subcategory: significant pairwise test with CI including zero
issues.description: The manuscript marks the Statistical vs Joint comparison for perceived impact as significant after Bonferroni correction (p=.041), but the reported 95% CI for d includes zero. This inconsistency suggests incorrect confidence interval computation, incorrect p-value, or mixing of metrics.

issues.subcategory: mismatch between ANOVA significance and pairwise conclusions
issues.description: The omnibus test for identifiability on perceived impact is significant, but the stated hypothesis predicted identifiable > statistical. The only significant pairwise difference is statistical vs joint, with no significant identifiable vs statistical effect. Yet the abstract and discussion language imply support for the extension hypothesis. This overstates the result and misaligns it with the tested prediction.
issues.quote: It is hypothesized that people generally perceive a stronger impact of donation towards an identified victim than unidentified statistical victims.

issues.subcategory: abstract claim contradicts reported pairwise results
issues.description: The abstract claims lower perceived impact when participants faced an identifiable victim or an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics, but the reported post-hoc tests only support a difference between statistical and joint conditions, not identifiable versus statistical. Thus the abstract overstates and misreports the findings.
issues.quote: Results have supported the hypothesis that people have a lower rating of perceived impact of donation when they faced an identifiable victim or an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics.

issues.subcategory: incorrect contrast test and degrees of freedom
issues.description: The manuscript compares one cell against the combination of all other cells using a t-test with df=998, but does not specify whether this was a planned contrast within ANOVA, whether variances/sample-size weighting were handled correctly, or how the pooled comparison was formed. The approach appears ad hoc and not directly comparable to the original contrast because the replication added extra conditions.
issues.quote: we also conducted a t-test to study if the mean of identifiable/no intervention condition is different from the mean of combining other five conditions on donation

issues.description: The study runs numerous omnibus ANOVAs, multiple post-hoc comparisons, and six condition-specific correlations across many outcomes. Aside from some Bonferroni-labeled pairwise comparisons, there is no clear familywise or false-discovery control across the full set of tests, increasing the chance of false positives.
issues.quote: Table 9 to 18 summarise statistical testings for the hypotheses of this replication... We conducted a correlation between aggregated feelings and donation ... across all conditions

issues.description: Several heterogeneous items (upset, touched, sympathetic, moral responsibility, donation appropriateness, and sometimes perceived impact) are treated as an aggregated feelings construct, but no rationale, scale composition, coding, reliability, or factor structure is reported. Some items are not affective states at all, weakening construct validity.
issues.quote: Identifiability and intervention on aggregated feelings Note: combine segregated feelings into one aggregated feeling ... Note: Segregated feelings include being upsetting, being touched, being sympathetic, moral responsibility, donation appropriateness, and perceived impact of donation (extension)

issues.subcategory: mixing affective, moral, and efficacy constructs
issues.description: The manuscript conceptually groups affective reactions with moral responsibility, donation appropriateness, and perceived impact. These are theoretically distinct constructs (emotion, norm judgment, efficacy belief). Aggregating or treating them interchangeably obscures mechanisms and undermines interpretation.
issues.quote: These items included beliefs about the severity of the crisis, the perceived trustworthiness of the charity, the expected accountability of funds, evaluation of organizational efficiency, and the appropriateness of donation to help the victims.

issues.subcategory: missing exact measures and response scales
issues.description: The manuscript does not report the exact wording, anchors, scale ranges, item order, coding direction, or whether donation was integer-constrained. It refers readers to external links/supplements instead of providing sufficient detail in the paper, hampering reproducibility and review.
issues.quote: For the full reported survey, please access the Qualtrics survey with the link below: https://www.dropbox.com/...

issues.description: No clear account is provided of how participants were assigned to conditions, in what sequence stimuli were presented, whether order was randomized, or whether allocation was concealed. This is especially problematic because the procedure section says participants selected their conditions.
issues.quote: The session of “Procedure” in the supplementary summarizes the procedure of the current replication study.

issues.description: Although the manuscript says participants with prior knowledge and failed attention checks were excluded, it does not report how many were excluded, from which conditions, or whether exclusions were preregistered and applied before analysis. In the context of simulated data, even these statements are uninterpretable.
issues.quote: Participants who indicated they had prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect were excluded, as well as those who failed the attention check.

issues.description: The manuscript provides no information on missing responses, partial completions, item-level nonresponse, or how missing data were handled analytically. Given multiple scales and online data collection, this omission limits assessment of bias and replicability.
issues.quote: All measures and manipulations conducted for this investigation are reported, and data collection was completed before analyses.

issues.description: The manuscript claims preregistration but does not summarize the preregistered hypotheses, exclusion rules, primary outcomes, or analysis plan in enough detail to assess adherence. Given major departures from the original and placeholder results, transparent linkage to preregistration is essential.
issues.quote: Pre-registration on the Open Science Framework | <https://osf.io/n4jkh/?view_only=d52771c7540a4a8f8051c8b430a6f15d>

issues.description: Because results were generated from random data to show what sections will look like, it is impossible to tell which analyses are truly preregistered versus reverse-engineered placeholders. This creates substantial ambiguity in researcher degrees of freedom and planned versus exploratory analyses.
issues.quote: Results were written using randomized dataset produced by Qualtrics to simulate what these sections will look like after data collection.

issues.description: The replication uses MTurk online workers rather than people intercepted in a university student center. This may be acceptable in some contexts, but the manuscript does not adequately discuss how differences in age, culture, online setting, and donation norms may moderate identifiable victim effects.
issues.quote: Participants will conduct an online survey in Qualtrics on the Mechanical Amazon Turk platform while the original study surveyed inside a student center of a university in Pennsylvania

issues.description: The reported generated sample has a mean age of 67.8 and range 18-120, which is highly unusual for MTurk and for the target population. Even if simulated, these demographics underscore that the reported dataset is not representative and any claims about replication or extension are not generalizable.
issues.quote: Mage = 67.80, SD=30.10 ... Age range (years) | Not specified | 18-120

issues.description: The manuscript alternates between 'generated from Qualtrics', 'computer (online)', and future plans to recruit on MTurk, making it unclear what sample, if any, the results pertain to. The results therefore cannot be tied to a concrete population or procedure.
issues.quote: A total of 1000 responses were generated from the Qualtrics for pre-registration ... Participants will conduct an online survey in Qualtrics on the Mechanical Amazon Turk platform

issues.description: Given the central claim concerns explicit learning about the identifiable victim effect and implicit deliberation via joint presentation, the study should verify that participants understood the intervention and that it changed deliberative processing. No manipulation checks are described.
issues.quote: Our first goal is to conduct independent (close) replications of the identifiable victim effect, particularly on debiasing the identifiable victim effect through inducing a calculative thinking mechanism.

issues.description: The manuscript interprets effects in terms of affective heuristic suppression and calculative thinking, but does not test mediation or process evidence linking manipulations to these mechanisms. Null or significant mean differences cannot establish that deliberation caused changes via reduced affect.
issues.quote: Reasoning about the choice of donation may suppress people’s automatic affective reaction towards the identifiable victim due to the perceived lack of effectiveness when contributing their money to a single individual.

issues.subcategory: joint condition changes phenomenon under study
issues.description: The original Study 3 concerned separate versus joint evaluation; by merging studies and applying intervention to the joint condition, the replication may no longer test the same theoretical phenomenon. The manuscript underplays that the joint condition itself is not just a third identifiability level but a different evaluative context.
issues.quote: The intervention of learning about the effect would also be applied to the joint condition to reveal a more comprehensive comparison between the explicit and implicit settings.

issues.description: The ANOVA summary tables report only a single df for each effect (e.g., identifiability df=2; intervention df=1; residual df=994) rather than standard numerator and denominator dfs together. This is nonstandard and hinders verification. For the original studies, dfs are also inconsistently represented across tables.
issues.quote: Variations | df | F | p | ηp2 | 95%CI ... Identifiability Replication | 2 | 3.58 | .028* | .007 | [0.00, 0.02]

issues.subcategory: confidence intervals for eta-squared not interpretable as presented
issues.description: The manuscript reports 95% CIs like [0.00, 0.02] alongside ηp2, but does not explain how these were computed. Since JAMOVI lacked this function and R was used, methodological transparency is needed. Given other inconsistencies, these CIs are difficult to trust and may not be standard for partial eta squared.
issues.quote: We conducted the data analysis with JAMOVI for statistical testing and R for calculation of 95%CI given that such function is not available for ANOVA testing in JAMOVI.

issues.subcategory: figures/tables referenced but incomplete or missing
issues.description: The manuscript references supplementary sections, figures, and tables that are not fully included or are placeholders. For example, cloud links are listed as '<enter link here>' and some table labels/descriptions are malformed. This undermines reviewability and reproducibility.
issues.quote:
Cloud folder for presentation (PPT and PDF) | <enter link here>
Cloud folder for peer reviews | <enter link here>

issues.description: The hypothesis table is poorly formatted, combining 5a and 5b in one row and mixing explicit and implicit intervention definitions. This creates ambiguity about what exact hypotheses were preregistered and tested.
issues.quote: 5a   5b | An identifiable victim elicits more affective feelings than an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics and statistical victims  Learning about the identifiable victim effect elicits less affective feelings towards an identifiable victim and identifiable victims with victim statistics but not towards statistical victims

issues.description: No internal consistency estimates (e.g., alpha/omega) are reported for aggregated feelings or any multi-item composites. Without reliability evidence, null findings or weak associations may reflect measurement error rather than absence of effects.
issues.quote: We conducted a 2 (intervention) X 3 (identifiability) two way ANOVA to examine the effect of identifiability and intervention on the aggregated feelings.

issues.description: Given the many deviations acknowledged in Table 6—different DV, physical setting, contextual variables, stimuli updates, added conditions, and combined studies—the classification as 'close to very close replication' appears overstated. This matters because conclusions about replication success depend on similarity to the original.
issues.quote: Replication classification | close to very close replication

issues.subcategory: extension hypothesis contradicts cited mixed literature
issues.description: The extension predicts higher perceived impact for identifiable victims, yet the cited literature immediately notes mixed or null findings. The manuscript does not sufficiently justify why this directional prediction is preferred over a non-directional hypothesis, especially after changing the donation task to hypothetical judgments.
issues.quote: Yet, there were mixed findings regarding the mediation effect of perceived impact on the identifiable victim effect... It is hypothesized that people generally perceive a stronger impact of donation towards an identified victim than unidentified statistical victims.
